== Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:531-660

\section{Declarations with Static Parameters}
\seclabel{overloading-static-params}

The rules above compare the parameter types and the return types of
declarations without static parameters.
A declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose parameter
type ranges over every instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their
bounds (\secref{overloading-terms}).
A declaration $d_1$ is more specific than a declaration $d_2$ when $d_2$ is
applicable to every call to which $d_1$ is applicable, and not the other way
round (\secref{resolving-overloading}); where neither has static parameters,
this is the relation $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$ of the rules above.
A set of overloaded declarations, some or all of which have static parameters,
is a valid overloading when every pair $d_1$, $d_2$ of them satisfies the
following three rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The \emph{No Duplicates Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each applicable to every
call to which the other is applicable.
\item
The \emph{Meet Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ exclude each other, or one of them is more
specific than the other, or some declaration of the set is more specific than
both and applicable to every call to which both are applicable.
\item
The \emph{Return Type Rule}: if $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$, then for
every argument type other than \TYP{BottomType} to which $d_1$ is applicable,
and for every instance of $d_2$ that is applicable to it, some instance of $d_1$
is applicable to it whose return type is a subtype of the return type of that
instance of $d_2$.
\end{itemize}
\revision{revival-overloading}{The revival's text of 30~September 2026 stated
the No Duplicates Rule as ``$d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each more specific than the
other'', which the strict sense of more specific above made refuse no pair.
It is stated on the relation without ``and not the other way round'', as the
type group's papers of 2011 and 2019 state it, and so it refuses
\EXP{\VAR{dup}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{Box}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket)}
beside \EXP{\VAR{dup}\llbracket{}U\rrbracket(x\COLON
\TYP{Box}\llbracket{}U\rrbracket)}, each applicable to every call to which the
other is.}
The Subtype Rule, the Incompatibility Rule and the Meet Rule above are these
rules for declarations without static parameters, with the conditions that
coercion adds; the Return Type Rule is the Subtype Rule's condition on return
types, checked over every instance of the less specific declaration and not
over one instance chosen for the pair.

As in \secref{more-specific-rule}, declarations of the set that are each more
specific than both $d_1$ and $d_2$ and that together cover every argument to
which both are applicable also satisfy the Meet Rule.
\revision{revival-meet}{The type group's paper of 2011 states the Meet Rule
without this case.}

Two parameter types with static parameters exclude each other, for the Meet
Rule and the Incompatibility Rule, as the type group's paper of 2011 decides it
by \emph{existential reduction}: each static parameter stands for any type
within its bound, and where the two parameter types mention one parameterized
trait, instantiation exclusion (\secref{trait-types}) lets them meet only where
the static arguments of those mentions are the same, every static argument but
an operator argument counting.
So where \TYP{Box} and \TYP{Pair} are distinct object types with static
parameters, the parameter types \EXP{\TYP{Box}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} and
\EXP{\TYP{Pair}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket} of two declarations exclude each
other whatever \VAR{T}, \VAR{A} and \VAR{B} stand for.

The Return Type Rule refuses the following pair, where trait \TYP{Round}
extends trait \TYP{Shape} and object \TYP{Circle} extends \TYP{Round}:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T = x
%ident(x: Round): Round = x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}(x\COLON \TYP{Round})\COLON \TYP{Round} = x\)
\end{Fortress}
The second declaration is more specific than the first.
For an argument of type \TYP{Circle}, the instance of the first at \TYP{Circle}
is applicable and returns a \TYP{Circle}, but the second, which runs for such an
argument, returns only a \TYP{Round}, and it has no other instance.
The pair is allowed when the second declaration is itself generic:
%ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T = x
%ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T = x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Round}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)
\end{Fortress}
Its instance at any type to which it is applicable returns that type.
\revision{revival-overloading}{This section is new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 required overloaded declarations to have
identical static parameters and ignored them.
The rules stated are those of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn,
Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple
Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011),
which the compiled type checker applies, with its Return Type Rule checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; the pair refused above has the
shape of that paper's own example, which the compiled path used to accept and
then fail to verify.
Neither implementation runs the pair allowed above today: the interpreter
refuses it at load, since it asks two declarations with static
parameters for a pair of parameter types that exclude each other (row~159 of the
revival's gap ledger), and the compiled code generator fails on it (row~537).
The compiled implementation adds one restriction that is not a rule of the
language.
When one declaration with static parameters is more specific than another that
declares as many static parameters of its own, the two must declare them of the
same kinds, position by position, and the return type of the more specific one
must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are identified
position by position; for its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
by position, to whichever declaration the call dispatches to (row~398 of the
revival's gap ledger).
So it refuses this override, whose return type names its static parameters in
the other order, where \TYP{Pr} is an object with two type parameters:
%trait Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\A, B\]
%end
%object M extends Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\B, A\] = Pr[\B, A\](1)
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Maker}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{make}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket()\COLON \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object} M \KWD{extends} \TYP{Maker}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{make}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket()\COLON \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}B, A\rrbracket = \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}B, A\rrbracket(1)\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
The type group's paper of 2019 (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019)
instantiates a dispatched declaration from the dynamic types of the arguments
and the static type of the call, renaming static parameters freely
(\secref{resolving-overloading}); under it the override is valid, and the
restriction goes when the compiled dispatcher instantiates a declaration that
way.}

== Specification/basic/traits.tex:413-681

\section{Method Declarations}
\seclabel{methods}

\note{
hidden without settable is a static error
only within traits
not  within objects !!!
-- Sukyoung}

\note{Accessing a field by a ``naked'' identifier reference
within trait declarations are not allowed.
We require a dotted field access by a ``self.'' prefix. (08/11/08)
-- Sukyoung}

\note{Getters must always be called with the special syntax:
\EXP{\VAR{receiver}.\VAR{getterName}
}

A getter is required to have a type consistent with a corresponding setter.}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{MdDecl} &::=& \emph{MdDef} \\
&$|$&
\option{\KWD{abstract}} \option{\emph{MdMods}} \option{\KWD{getter}}
\emph{MdHeaderFront} \emph{FnHeaderClause} \\

\emph{MdDef}  &::=& \option{\emph{MdMods}} \option{\KWD{getter}}
\emph{MdHeaderFront} \emph{FnHeaderClause}
\EXP{=} \emph{Expr} \\

\emph{AbsMdDecl} &::=&
\option{\KWD{abstract}} \option{\emph{AbsMdMods}} \option{\KWD{getter}}
\emph{MdHeaderFront} \emph{FnHeaderClause} \\

\emph{MdMods} &::=& \emph{MdMod}$^+$\\

\emph{MdMod} &::=& \emph{FnMod} $|$ \KWD{override}\\

\emph{FnMod} &::=& \emph{AbsFnMod} $|$ \KWD{private}\\

\emph{AbsFnMod} &::=& \emph{LocalFnMod} $|$
\KWD{test}\\

\emph{LocalFnMod} &::=& \KWD{atomic} $|$ \KWD{io}\\

\emph{AbsMdMods} &::=& \emph{AbsMdMod}$^+$\\

\emph{AbsMdMod} &::=& \emph{AbsFnMod} $|$ \KWD{override}\\

\emph{GetterSetterDecl} &::=& \emph{GetterSetterDef} \\
&$|$& \option{\KWD{abstract}} \option{\emph{FnMods}}
\emph{GetterSetterMod} \emph{MdHeaderFront} \emph{FnHeaderClause} \\

\emph{GetterSetterDef}  &::=& \option{\emph{FnMods}} \emph{GetterSetterMod}
\emph{MdHeaderFront} \emph{FnHeaderClause}
\EXP{=} \emph{Expr} \\

\emph{GetterSetterMod} &::=& \KWD{getter} $|$ \KWD{setter}\\

\emph{AbsGetterSetterDecl} &::=& \option{\KWD{abstract}} \option{\emph{AbsFnMods}}
 \emph{GetterSetterMod} \emph{MdHeaderFront} \emph{FnHeaderClause} \\

\emph{MdHeaderFront}  &::=& \emph{NamedMdHeaderFront}\\
&$|$& \emph{OpMdHeaderFront} \\

\emph{NamedMdHeaderFront} &::=&
\emph{Id} \option{\emph{StaticParams}} \emph{MdValParam} \\

\emph{MdValParam} &::=& \texttt( \option{\emph{MdParams}} \texttt) \\

\emph{MdParams}
&::=&
(\emph{MdParam}\EXP{,})$^*$ \options{\emph{Varargs}\EXP{,}} \emph{MdKeyword}(\EXP{,}\emph{MdKeyword})$^*$\\
&$|$&
(\emph{MdParam}\EXP{,})$^*$  \emph{Varargs}\\
&$|$& \emph{MdParam}(\EXP{,} \emph{MdParam})$^*$\\

\emph{MdKeyword} &::=& \emph{MdParam}\EXP{=}\emph{Expr} \\

\emph{MdParam} &::=& \emph{Param} \\
&$|$& \KWD{self} \\

\emph{Param} &::=& \emph{PlainParam}\\

\emph{PlainParam} &::=& \emph{BindId} \option{\emph{IsType}} \\
&$|$& \emph{Type} \\

\emph{FnHeaderClause} &::=& \option{\emph{IsType}} \emph{FnClauses} \\

\emph{IsType} &::=& \EXP{\mathrel{\mathtt{:}}} \emph{Type}\\

\emph{FnClauses} &::=& \option{\emph{Throws}} \option{\emph{Where}} \emph{Contract} \\

\emph{Throws} &::=& \KWD{throws} \emph{MayTraitTypes}\\

\emph{MayTraitTypes} &::=& \texttt{\{\}} \\
&$|$& \emph{TraitTypes} \\

\end{Grammar}

A trait declaration contains a set of method declarations.
Syntactically, a method declaration begins with
an optional sequence of modifiers followed by
the method's name,
optional static parameters
(described in \chapref{trait-parameters}),
the value parameter with its (optionally) declared type,
an optional type of a return value,
an optional declaration of thrown checked exceptions
(discussed in \chapref{exceptions}),
an optional \KWD{where} clause
(discussed in \secref{where-clauses}),
a contract for the method (discussed in \secref{method-contracts}),
and finally an optional body expression preceded by the token \EXP{=}.
If a method declaration has the \KWD{getter} modifier,
it does not affect the behavior of a program; rather,
it documents that the method is intended to serve as a getter.
A \KWD{throws} clause does not include naked type variables.
Every element in a \KWD{throws} clause is a subtype of
\TYP{CheckedException}.


Method declarations can include the following special modifiers:
\paragraph{\KWD{getter}:}
A method declaration with the modifier \KWD{getter} explicitly declares a
getter method for a field, even in the absence of an actual field declaration.
\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}
If such a field exists, there is no implicit getter for the field.
An explicitly declared getter method must take no arguments and return a
result of the field's type.
A getter method must not throw any checked exception.
Getter names may not overlap ordinary method names.
A getter method must be invoked with the field access syntax:
%expr.id
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{expr}.\VAR{id}\)
\end{Fortress}
where \VAR{id} is the name of the getter method.



\paragraph{\KWD{setter}:}
A method declaration with the modifier \KWD{setter} explicitly declares a
setter method for a field, even in the absence of an actual field.
\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}
If such a field exists, there is no implicit setter for the field.
An explicitly declared setter method must take a single argument---the
value being set---and return \EXP{()}.
A setter method must not throw any checked exception.
Setter names may not overlap ordinary method names.
A setter method must be invoked with the \emph{assignment syntax}:
%expr1.id := expr2
\begin{Fortress}
\({expr}_{1}.\VAR{id} \ASSIGN {expr}_{2}\)
\end{Fortress}


We say that a method declaration \emph{occurs} in a trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{declares} a method declaration that occurs
in that trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{inherits} method declarations from the
declarations of its immediate supertraits
except those method declarations
that are \emph{overridden} (as described later in this section) or
whose parameter type (not including the type of the self parameter)
is equal to the parameter type of a method declaration
that occurs in the trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{provides} the method declarations that it
declares or inherits.




There are two sorts of method declarations:
\emph{dotted method} declarations and
\emph{functional method} declarations.
Syntactically, a dotted method declaration is identical to a function
declaration.
When a method is invoked, a special self parameter is bound to the
object on which it is invoked.



A functional method declaration has a parameter named \KWD{self} at an
arbitrary position in its parameter list.  This parameter is not given a type
and implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object.
\revision{revival-self-type}{In a trait \VAR{T} with a self-type parameter \VAR{X}
(\secref{trait-decls}), this remains the type of the \KWD{self} parameter
in the declaration's signature, which overloading and the choice of a declaration
at a call read; in the method's body \KWD{self} has the type \EXP{T \cap X}
(\secref{idn-ref}).}
Semantically, functional method declarations can be viewed as top-level
function declarations.  For example, the following overloaded functional method
\VAR{f} declared within a trait declaration \VAR{A}:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.a.tex}
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.b.tex}
may be rewritten as top-level functions as follows:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.c.tex}
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.d.tex}
where \VAR{internalF} is a freshly generated name.
Functional method declarations may be overloaded with top-level function
declarations.
An abstract function declaration
(described in \secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations})
can be provided also for overloaded functional method declarations.
See \chapref{multiple-dispatch} for a discussion of overloaded
functionals in Fortress.

When a method declaration includes a body expression, it is called a
\emph{method definition}.
A method declaration that does not have its body expression is referred to
as an \emph{abstract method declaration}.
An abstract method declaration declares an \emph{abstract method};
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method: a method definition with the same name and the self parameter (if any)
at the same position whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self
parameter, is that of the abstract method declaration, or definitions whose
parameter types are subtypes of it and together cover it
(\secref{internal-types}), or it is a static error.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said only that
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method.
The object defines the method by a body at its parameter type, or by bodies at
narrower parameter types that together cover it, \KWD{comprises} clauses read
at the level of values (\secref{trait-decls}), as
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} asks of the concrete declarations for an
abstract function declaration; one body at a narrower parameter type that does
not cover the abstract method's does not define it.
This is the rule of the type group's compiled type checker (2012) and of its
calculus Welterweight Fortress (2012).
The requirement of \secref{object-decls} that an object define all abstract
methods inherited from its supertraits is unchanged: it defines them in this
sense.}
An abstract method declaration may include the modifier \KWD{abstract}.
It may elide parameter names but parameter
types cannot be omitted except for the self parameter.


\note{
Method declarations that are overridden by some declaration are not
accessible.  They are not considered for overloading checks.

Partial overriding of an overloaded functional is allowed
but partial overriding of a functional declaration is not allowed.
}

A method declaration may have the modifier \KWD{override}.
Such a declaration \emph{overrides} any inherited declaration with the same name
and the self parameter (if any) at the same position,
whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self parameter,
is a strict subtype of the overriding declaration's parameter type.
The return type of the overriding declaration must be subtype of
that of the overridden declaration to preserve type safety.
A declaration with the modifier \KWD{override} must override
some inherited declaration.
It is a static error if a declaration with the modifier \KWD{override}
does not override any inherited declaration.

Here is an example trait \TYP{Enzyme} which provides methods
\VAR{reactionSpeed} and \VAR{catalyze}:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.e.tex}
\TYP{Enzyme}
inherits the abstract method \VAR{mass} from \TYP{OrganicMolecule},
declares the abstract method \VAR{reactionSpeed}, and
declares the concrete method \VAR{catalyze}
which is inherited as an abstract method
from its supertrait \TYP{Catalyst}.

== Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2362-2565

\subsection{Overloading with static parameters}
\seclabel{revival-overloading}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{overloading-terms};
\secref{functional-applicability}; \secref{dotted-method-applicability};
\secref{resolving-overloading}; \secref{principles-overloading};
\secref{overloading-static-params}; \secref{resolving-coercion}; and, in a
draft build, the proposed features of the appendix ``Internal Document''.
\item[Change] The sentence of \secref{overloading-terms} that declarations of
one name may not differ in their static parameters, and its echo in
\secref{principles-overloading}, are replaced: declarations of one name may have
different static parameters, or some of them static parameters and others none,
and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose
parameter type ranges over its instances.
Such a declaration is applicable to a call when some instance of it within its
bounds is, and it is compared with others on the parameter types they declare,
taken over all their instances; the static arguments that a call does not write
are inferred for the declaration it selects, after the selection
(\chapref{type-inference}).
The three sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} that inferred static
parameters before applicability was checked and before declarations were
compared, and the chapter's assumption that the static variables of a call have
been instantiated or inferred, are rewritten to match.
A new section, \secref{overloading-static-params}, states for declarations with
static parameters the three rules of the type group's paper of 2011, the No
Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule, the last checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; how two parameter types with
static parameters exclude each other, by existential reduction with
instantiation exclusion; and a pair that the Return Type Rule refuses, in the
shape of that paper's own example, beside the pair that repairs it.
A box in that section states the restriction that the compiled implementation
adds, that of two declarations with as many static parameters of their own, one
of which is more specific than the other, the two agree on their static
parameters position by position, with an override that reorders them as its
example.
A later revision states the section's No Duplicates Rule on the relation without
``and not the other way round'', that $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each applicable to
every call to which the other is applicable, with a box, and the box on Jan's
example in the internal document gives that rule as its reason.
\secref{resolving-coercion} says in three places that a declaration with static
parameters is applicable when some instance of it is, that it is compared on the
parameter types it declares, and that the declaration selected is then
instantiated, the coercions of its instance inserted statically.
In the internal document, the proposed features on relaxing the restrictions on
the static parameters of overloaded functionals and on overloading with static
parameters are marked done, Jan's example answered by \library's factory and the
questions on exclusion by the existential reduction.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 26~September 2026 that the sentence goes and that this working draft states
the model of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick,
Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple Dispatch
with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011;
\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 132--180, and
\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/setup.tick}, lines 393--397, in the revival's
repository), which the compiled type checker applies, with two changes to the
checker: the Return Type Rule checked over every instance, and the positional
restriction.
On 28~September 2026 it decided that a coercion makes a call possible and never
changes which declaration runs when one is applicable without it, declarations
being chosen on the parameter types they declare and the declaration chosen
being then instantiated.
Neither implementation enforced the sentence: the interpreter has overloaded
declarations with different static parameters since May 2007, the compiled type
checker applies the rules of that paper to them, and \library\ overload across
different static parameters throughout.
The sentence is text of 2009.
The Fortress~1.0 release of 2008 compared generic declarations instead by
using ``their bounds as their supertypes'', in a section whose type relations
``may be replaced when the static type checker and the type inference engine
are implemented'' (\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf},
Section~15.6.1), and the team's unfinished restart of this specification in
2012 dropped the sentence
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/overloading.tick},
lines 100--114, in the revival's repository).
The restart's Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) gives function types that hold
generic and plain declarations together, as sets of arrow types and universal
arrow types, and drops from a quantified type a static parameter that appears
in none of its types
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
553--558, 764--767 and 794--801).
The positional restriction is the compiled implementation's and not the
language's: its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
by position, to whichever declaration dispatch reaches (row~398 of the
revival's gap ledger), while the type group's paper of 2019 instantiates a
dispatched declaration by substitution and renames static parameters freely
(Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, ``Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with
Variance'', POPL 2019, Sections~4 and~5.2).
That paper's soundness proof excludes an upper bound that names a type
parameter, its own included, and closed types, so that \library's families over a type parameter
bounded by an instance of a trait at itself, such as \STR{SUM}, \STR{BIG~MAX}
and those over \TYP{Integral}, rest on the rules of 2011 as the compiled type
checker implements them, and not on the proof of 2019.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
The No Duplicates Rule was first stated on the strict sense of more specific
that the section defines, under which no two declarations are each more
specific than the other, so that it refused no pair, and two declarations each
applicable to every call to which the other is fell to the Meet Rule (row~696
of the revival's gap ledger).
The paper of 2011 defines its relation of specificity without strictness, one
declaration being more specific than another when every type to which the first
is applicable is one to which the second is, and its No Duplicates Rule
``forbids distinct declarations from being equally specific''
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 97--108, 158--162 and 184--185);
the paper of 2019 states it as ``Distinct method declarations must have
different applicable sets'' (Section~2.2), and its rules [No-Dup-Not-Less] and
[No-Dup-Not-Gtr] refuse exactly a pair whose domain types are each a subtype of
the other (Section~4.1 and Figure~5).
The restatement follows the revival's decision of 23~September 2026 that the
type group's later word, that paper among it, outweighs the early text; its
reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] Declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters,
as \library's do.
The compiled type checker refuses the pair of the Return Type Rule's example,
which it accepted before and whose compiled class then failed verification, and
an override whose return type reorders its static parameters, which it accepted
before and which then failed at run time (row~398).
Neither implementation runs every set these rules allow.
The compiled type checker refuses more than the Return Type Rule where the more
specific declaration's parameter type is an object type, as in
\EXP{\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T} beside
\EXP{\VAR{ident}(x\COLON \TYP{Circle})\COLON \TYP{Circle}} where \TYP{Circle} is an
object (row~542); the compiled code generator fails on two declarations with
static parameters whose bounds differ, the pair the Return Type Rule allows in
\secref{overloading-static-params} among them, and on the example of the type
group's paper of 2019 that overloads a method over an array list and a list
(row~537); and the interpreter refuses at load two declarations with static
parameters of which no pair of parameter types excludes each other (row~159),
that example among them (row~539).
Jan's example is still not a valid overloading, its two declarations having the
same parameter type.
The compiled type checker applies the No Duplicates Rule as it is now stated:
it refuses two declarations whose parameter types, read over their instances,
are each a subtype of the other, ``There are multiple declarations of \VAR{dup}
with the same parameter type'', except two functional methods whose \KWD{self}
parameters stand at different positions, which only its code generator
refuses, as a malformed overload set (row~707 of the revival's gap ledger).
The interpreter loads such a pair and runs one of them where both declarations
have static parameters and their parameter types mention one parameterized
type, as \VAR{dup}'s do (row~373), and where one has static parameters and the
other's parameter type is its bound (row~549).
The calculus of \appref{overloading-calculus} keeps its rule that two
declarations with the same number of parameters have static parameters with the
same bounds; it admits fewer overloadings than these chapters, so that its valid
programs are still valid, and its rules and its soundness claim are unchanged
(\secref{revival-calculi}).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/overloading.tex},
lines 100--108:
\begin{quote}
Although there may be multiple declarations with the same functional name,
it is an error for their static parameters to differ (up to
$\alpha$-equivalence), or for one declaration to have static parameters and
another to not have them.
Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which
declarations are applicable, so we ignore them for most of this chapter.
\end{quote}
lines 137--138:
\begin{quote}
We assume throughout this chapter that all static variables in functional calls
have been instantiated or inferred.
\end{quote}
lines 173--175, and in the same words for the types $\Ps_0$ and $\Ps$ of a
dotted method declaration, lines 205--207:
\begin{quote}
If the parameter type $\Ps$ includes static parameters, they are inferred as
described in \chapref{type-inference} before checking the applicability of the
declaration to the call.
\end{quote}
lines 292--295:
\begin{quote}
If the declarations include static parameters, they are inferred as described
in \chapref{type-inference} before comparing their parameter types to determine
which declaration is more specific.
\end{quote}
and \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced/overloading.tex}, lines
95--103:
\begin{quote}
Overloaded declarations must have static parameters that are identical (up to
$\alpha$-equivalence).  Also, valid overloadings for declarations that contain
keyword or varargs parameters are determined by analyzing the expansion of these
declarations as described in \secref{applicability-with-special-params}.
Therefore, static parameters, keyword parameters, and varargs parameters are
ignored in the remainder of this chapter.
\end{quote}
The sentences added to \secref{resolving-coercion}, after the Working Draft's
lines 455--459, 522--524 and 567--570 of
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/conversions-coercions.tex}, and the new
section have no counterpart there.
The new section, the revival's text of 30~September 2026, stated:
\begin{quote}
The \emph{No Duplicates Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each more specific than
the other.
\end{quote}
and the box on Jan's example in the internal document gave as its reason that
the two declarations have the same parameter type ``and each is more specific
than the other''.
\item[Route C] The same under route~C, except that the existential reduction
uses the rule of \secref{revival-routec} in place of instantiation exclusion;
the No Duplicates Rule does not depend on the rule on instantiations.
\end{description}

== Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2748-2935

\subsection{Traits with comprises clauses read at the level of values}
\seclabel{revival-covering}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{internal-types};
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}; \secref{methods}; a draft note in the
subsection ``Export Statements'' of \secref{components}; the effect of
\secref{revival-comprises}.
\item[Change] \secref{internal-types} defines covering: a type covers another
when every value of the second is a value of the first; a type covers each of
its subtypes, and a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause is covered by the union
of its listed types; covering is not the subtype relation.
Its example concludes that $V$ covers $S \inter T$, where it concluded that
$V = S \inter T$, and a sentence says that a trait may stand between $S$ or $T$
and their listed types, so that $S \inter T$ is not in general equal to a named
type.
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} asks the argument types of the concrete
declarations to cover the argument type of the abstract declaration, where it
asked their union to equal it, and, in its example, for a definition for every
type listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause of \TYP{Molecule} or definitions that
together cover those types, where it asked for one for every immediate subtype.
Each of these four passages has a box.
The draft note says ``all its listed types'' where it said ``all its immediate
subtraits''; a draft note prints only in a draft build, so it has no box.
The effect of \secref{revival-comprises} no longer says that these passages are
not revised.
A correction of 9~October 2026 changes the last sentence of the box after the
example in \secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} and the sentence of this
entry's effect that repeats it.
They said that the compiled type checker checks that an object's concrete
methods cover the abstract methods it inherits, ``reading no \KWD{comprises}
clause''; they now say that it reads such clauses to do so, so that concrete
methods over the types that a trait lists together cover an abstract method
over that trait.
The normative text is unchanged.
An amendment of 14~October 2026 revises the sentence of \secref{methods} on
abstract methods: an object inheriting an abstract method defines it by a method
definition whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self parameter, is
that of the abstract method declaration, or by definitions whose parameter types
are subtypes of it and together cover it, or it is a static error, where the
sentence said only that the object must define a body expression for the method.
The sentence has a box.
The requirement of \secref{object-decls} that an object define all abstract
methods inherited from its supertraits is unchanged; the box says that it is
read in this sense.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 29~September 2026 that the passages that read a \KWD{comprises} clause at the
level of types are restated at the level of values, which is how
\secref{trait-decls} reads the clause since its revision of 28~September 2026
(\secref{revival-comprises}).
The team's later Types chapter names covering beside subtyping and exclusion as
a relation between types, and says that an instantiation of a trait with a
\KWD{comprises} clause ``is covered by the union'' of the listed types
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines 36--38
and 384--390, in the revival's repository).
Welterweight Fortress, the type group's calculus of 2012, reads the clause at
the level of values and counts an abstract declaration as covered when it is
implemented for all the types comprised
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick}, lines 21--22;
\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/fig-covered.tick}).
Under that reading a trait with static parameters may stand unlisted between a
trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types; an instantiation of it
is then a subtype of the closed trait and of no listed type, though every value
of it is a value of a listed type, so the passages' conclusions hold of values
and not of types.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
and \nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-judgement.md} in the
revival's repository.
The sentence that the correction of 9~October 2026 changes was false when it was
written: since 6~June 2012 the team's compiled type checker, testing whether an
abstract method's parameter type is a subtype of the union of the parameter
types of the concrete methods below it, tests whether the union of the types
that a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause lists is a subtype of that union
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/AbstractMethodChecker.scala}
and \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala},
in the revival's repository).
It accepts an object whose methods over the two types that a trait lists cover
an abstract method over that trait, and refuses the same object when the trait
has no \KWD{comprises} clause.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-override/REPORT.md} in the
revival's repository.
The amendment of 14~October 2026 follows the revival's decision of 13~October
2026 that an object defines an inherited abstract method when its definitions
of that name at narrower parameter types together cover the abstract method's
parameter types, \KWD{comprises} clauses read as the compiled type checker
reads them; a definition at the abstract method's own parameter type is the
plain case.
It is the type group's rule of 2012.
The compiled type checker checks, at each object declaration, whether each
inherited abstract method ``is covered by one or more concrete definitions'',
its parameter type a subtype of the union of theirs (Steele, May 2012, in
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/AbstractMethodChecker.scala},
in the revival's repository), and reads \KWD{comprises} clauses to do so since
6~June 2012.
Welterweight Fortress uses the same rules to check methods as functions, the
type of the trait or object within which the method is declared not considered
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/static.tick}, lines 27--47).
The sentence of \secref{methods} is older than that reading; the chapter's own
sentence on overloaded functional methods points to
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}, which asks for coverage, as the Meet Rule
does.
The team's library and tests define abstract methods by covering definitions:
the trait \TYP{RunRanges} of the component \TYP{Pairs}
(\nolinkurl{Library/Pairs.fss}) and the trait \TYP{dna} of the test
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/FileConversion.fss}, which the sentence read to
the letter would refuse.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/walk-load-readings-check.md}, section~2, in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] No example of this specification becomes invalid.
Covering is not subtyping: where an instantiation of a trait with static
parameters stands between $S$ and $T$ and their listed types, its value is a
value of $V$ but its static type is not a subtype of $V$, and the compiled type
checker refuses to assign it to a variable of type $V$; the interpreter, which
has no static types, runs such an assignment.
The compiled type checker checks, at each object declaration, that the
object's concrete methods cover the abstract methods it inherits, and reads
\KWD{comprises} clauses to do so: concrete methods over the types that a trait
lists together cover an abstract method over that trait; top-level abstract
function declarations run on neither implementation.
Since the amendment of 14~October 2026 the interpreter checks the same at load,
at each object without static parameters, reading \KWD{comprises} clauses as its
check of the Meet Rule reads them: it accepts an object whose definitions at
narrower parameter types together cover an inherited abstract method, as before,
and refuses one whose definitions do not cover it, where it accepted any one
definition at narrower parameter types before.
It does not check objects with static parameters and object expressions in
generic functions (row~665 of the revival's gap ledger), and it
does not refuse an object where its search through the \KWD{comprises} clauses
does not settle: a cycle, its bound on steps or parts, or a type it cannot read;
it then loads an object that the compiled type checker refuses (row~708 of the
revival's gap ledger).
The compiled type checker does not split a tuple of parameter types through
\KWD{comprises} clauses: it refuses an object whose concrete methods cover an
inherited abstract method of two parameters only through combinations of the
types that a trait lists, which the interpreter accepts (row~709 of the
revival's gap ledger).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex},
lines 568--570:
\begin{quote}
because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
clause of $U$, any subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of $V$.  Thus,
$V = S \inter T$.
\end{quote}
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/functions.tex}, lines 377--378:
\begin{quote}
Furthermore, the union of the argument types of the concrete declarations for
\VAR{f} must be equal to \VAR{T}.
\end{quote}
and lines 413--415:
\begin{quote}
For the latter, the programmer must provide a definition for every immediate
subtype of \TYP{Molecule}, or it is a static error.
\end{quote}
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/components/source-code.tex}, line
429, the words of the draft note's second item that changed:
\begin{quote}
provided that all its immediate subtraits are considered to have concrete
method declaration with that signature.
\end{quote}
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, lines 510--512:
\begin{quote}
An abstract method declaration declares an \emph{abstract method}; any object
inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the method.
\end{quote}

entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

content.content:
# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run time

The code of this area is in these directories:

- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.

The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.

## What the two paths share

After the phases, each path has its own code for these:

- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
- Number natives: walk's `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`), and the compiled `nativeHelpers/` (`simpleIntArith.java`).
- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.

The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.

## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over

The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.

Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay.

## What the compiled path cannot compile yet

For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:

- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.

It also refuses a function, object or trait declaration with a `where` clause or a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private` and `abstract`, such as `override` (ledger row 650).

The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.

Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).

## What the code generator does

`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time", gives the jars, the dispatch methods, the templates and the boxed numbers.

- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet (`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time"). If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:Storage is' 'positions:array design'

## The run time

- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.

## Natives

`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.

The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.

## Traps of the compiled path

- Before disambiguation, the compiled path bounds an unbounded type parameter by `Object`, not `Any`. Walk does not. So the compiled path rejects every generic that is instantiated at a tuple type, until the switch-over (ledger row 412).
- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.

## The `fortress` commands

`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

## Running

    cd ProjectFortress
    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.

- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead: it gives the cause.

## Before an edit

Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. Both date from September 2026, so a status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.

- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'

- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the run time and B.12 the natives.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'

- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.

## Testing an edit here

- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. This takes seconds, rebuilds nothing and changes nothing tracked. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:

      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
      bin/fortress run P

  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).

content.content:
# The interpreter (walk)

Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:

- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
- `glue/`: the natives.

## How walk evaluates a program

After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.

At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.

Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.

## Where a fix of walk belongs

Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:

- coercion;
- chained comparisons;
- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.

Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.

An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.

## What walk checks

Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It refuses:

- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if their declared domains order a generic declaration and a plain one, or if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap.
- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`) in a type that provides both.
- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses.
- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. If walk's search for a cover does not settle, it does not refuse.
- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.

  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.

So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:

- adds an overload;
- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover;
- adds an `override` that overrides nothing.

`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.

Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.

## Natives

The library binds each of walk's natives by a string in its `.fss` files: `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X")`. The classes are in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. They take the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use them. `import java`, the compiled path's way to bind natives, is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it.

To raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees, a native throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `Int.java` there makes one, and its callers throw it:

    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
    return new FortressError(f);

A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other exception from a native ends the run, a division by zero too.

## Running a program

    bin/fortress P.fss

- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.

## The model program

MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.

- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.

(* An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies at narrower parameter types that together cover the abstract method's parameter types, a comprises clause read at the level of values, so the program loads and runs, under walk (traits.tex, section "Method Declarations"). *)

  g(self, x: P, y: Q): ZZ32 = 12
  g(self, x: Q, y: D): ZZ32 = 13
end

    assert(f(P, Q), 2, "f over P and Q")

== explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md:365-375

## B.7 Overloading

Resolution is split between a shared rewrite and two completely different dispatch mechanisms.

The shared part: `OverloadRewriter` replaces a reference that has several candidates with a reference to a single synthetic name spelled `f{f1,f2,…}` and appends a `_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` declaring it (`compiler/OverloadRewriter.java:74-92`, `OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:110-142`).

On the interpreter path, `BuildTopLevelEnvironments.for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` (`interpreter/evaluator/BuildTopLevelEnvironments.java:128`) turns that declaration into an `OverloadedFunction`, and the actual selection happens per call, on run-time values, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatch` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:787`); failure is the familiar "Failed to find any matching overload" (`:795`).

On the compiler path, `CodeGen.for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6409`) hands the declaration to `OverloadSet`, which emits one dispatch method per overloaded name, testing argument types from most to least specific (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1944,1964`).

So the same phase feeds a run-time search in one world and a generated decision tree in the other, and the candidate lists they start from are different (`OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:107`): the interpreter's comes from the disambiguator, the compiler's from the type checker.
